body:
You walk into a Pre-Intermediate class of 16 adults at a language academy. It's your third lesson with them. You've planned a warm-up discussion on 'memorable journeys' — an open question designed to get everyone speaking.

Thirty seconds in, Maria — a confident, extroverted learner — has already taken over. She's telling a long, animated story about her trip to Thailand. Three other students are trying to get a word in. The quieter ones in the back have given up and are looking at their phones.

You have 90 minutes and an entire lesson to deliver. What do you do?

During a fluency-focused group discussion on 'future plans', you're monitoring and hear several errors:

  • "I will going to university next year"
  • "If I will have time, I travel more"
  • "She go to work by bus every day"

Students are engaged, speaking freely, and building on each other's ideas. The grammar errors are systematic — your class has first-language interference from their shared L1.

You're trained in both fluency-first and accuracy-first approaches. How do you handle correction here?

Next week, you're teaching a new Upper-Intermediate class with a mix of learners: 4 university students preparing for IELTS, 3 business professionals who need English for emails and meetings, and 2 retired learners studying for personal enrichment.

The topic is 'expressing opinions and justifying arguments' — for CEFR B2 speaking. You need to decide your core teaching approach for this mixed-purpose group.

Which methodology do you choose?

You're drilling the Present Perfect with controlled practice. You ask: "How many countries has Anna visited?"

A learner, Ahmed, confidently answers: "She have visited three countries."

This is the third time this lesson Ahmed has dropped the third-person 's' — a classic L1 transfer issue for Arabic speakers. The class can hear the error. Ahmed is a diligent learner who values correctness and often loses confidence when corrected publicly.

The coursebook is watching; you have 12 more controlled practice items to get through. What's your move?

Mid-lesson, during a pair-work communicative activity, one learner — Pablo — pushes his chair back, folds his arms, and says loudly: "This is pointless. I don't pay money to talk to other students. I pay money to talk to the teacher."

The room goes quiet. Other learners look at you, waiting to see how you handle it. Pablo is a senior executive in his 40s, used to being in control. He's been resistant since Lesson 1 and his attitude is starting to affect the class dynamic.

You have 45 minutes left. The communicative activity was designed to take 15 of those and leads into a freer speaking task. How do you respond?

You're teaching a multi-level Elementary class with a wide range: three absolute beginners who can barely say their names, five 'false beginners' who studied English years ago, and two learners who should clearly be in Pre-Intermediate.

The coursebook has you on Unit 4: 'Daily Routines' — present simple with I/you/we/they. The beginners are lost during the presentation. The stronger pair finishes every exercise in 30 seconds and starts chatting in L1.

Your DoS (Director of Studies) has told you to 'follow the syllabus.' How do you manage this spread?

You're in your second week at a new language academy. One learner — Elena — consistently submits ChatGPT-generated homework. The vocabulary is C1 level in an Intermediate class, and the sentence structures don't match her spoken production at all.

You've checked the academy policy: there is a generic 'academic integrity' clause in the enrolment contract, but no specific AI policy has been communicated to teachers or students. Other teachers in the staff room say 'just ignore it — she's not hurting anyone.'

The homework is 10% of the course grade. Elena is a well-liked, motivated student who participates actively in class. What do you do?

It's Week 6 of 10. You have a quiet, diligent learner — Mei — who has completed every homework assignment, participates when called on, and scores 80-90% on all tests. She seems to be progressing well.

During a one-to-one needs analysis meeting, Mei starts crying. Through tears, she tells you: 'I understand everything in class. I do well on your tests. But when I try to speak to real English people — at the supermarket, in a taxi — I freeze. I can't say anything. I've been studying for six years and I still can't have a conversation.'

Her test scores tell you she's succeeding. Her lived experience tells you she's not. How do you address this gap?

Your academy runs 60-minute lessons. You have a teenage learner, Diego (15), who has been diagnosed with ADHD. His mother disclosed this to you privately and asked you to 'help him focus.' Diego is bright, has good receptive vocabulary, but struggles to sit still during any task lasting more than 4-5 minutes.

The coursebook lesson today involves a 10-minute reading comprehension followed by 8 comprehension questions. By minute 3, Diego is tapping his pen, swivelling in his chair, and staring at the ceiling. The other 5 students in this small group are adults who are visibly distracted.

You can't redesign the entire curriculum. What adjustments do you make, right now?

You're planning your next lesson for an Upper-Intermediate class. The topic from the coursebook is 'The Environment' — a standard lesson with a reading passage about recycling, some vocabulary matching, and a discussion question at the end.

You know your class well: they are more engaged when lessons connect to their local context. Several learners work in local industries, and two are employed by a company that has been in the news for a recent environmental controversy.

The coursebook material is safe, pre-approved, and requires minimal preparation. Creating localised materials would take you an extra 2 hours tonight. Do you adapt the lesson?

You give a mid-course speaking test to your Pre-Intermediate class. The test has three criteria: Fluency & Coherence, Lexical Resource, and Grammatical Range & Accuracy. Each is scored 1-5.

Anna gives a confident, engaging 2-minute response to the prompt. She uses a wide range of vocabulary — some of it above her level. She makes 6 grammatical errors (mostly third-person 's' and irregular past tense). She communicates her ideas clearly and the message is never lost.

You need to give her a score. Your academy expects 'consistent, standardised marking.' What overall score do you give Anna, and why?

You've just finished a controlled practice activity — a gap-fill on conditional sentences. You circulate to check answers and notice that almost every student has made the same error on item 5: they've written 'If I would have...' instead of 'If I had...'

This is a common L1 transfer error for this nationality, and it's persistent. You planned to move on to the freer practice stage in 3 minutes. Your lesson aim for today is 'functional use of conditionals for giving advice.'

Half the class hasn't mastered the form yet. The other half has finished and is waiting. What's your next move?

You teach a Business English one-to-one learner, Klaus, a senior engineer at an automotive firm. He needs English for: (1) writing technical emails to German colleagues, (2) presenting at quarterly international meetings, and (3) small talk at work dinners.

Klaus has told you clearly: 'I do not want games. I do not want role-plays. I want to study grammar, read technical articles, and build my vocabulary. I am paying for results.'

Research tells you that communicative, task-based approaches produce better long-term outcomes for speaking confidence. But Klaus is your client, and he's explicit about what he wants. How do you reconcile these?

Your academy has a mandatory final exam that counts for 60% of the course grade. The exam is a standardised 100-question multiple-choice test covering grammar, vocabulary, and reading — exactly the kind of test that rewards passive recognition, not active production.

You believe in communicative language teaching. Your lessons have been built around speaking, meaningful interaction, and task-based learning. Your learners have made real progress in fluency and confidence.

But the exam doesn't test any of that. If they fail, the academy may hold you accountable. How do you prepare them?

During a free writing task — 'describe a person who has influenced you' — one of your adult learners, Yuki, submits a paragraph about her former university professor. The paragraph is well written, well organised, and emotionally powerful. It describes how the professor 'changed her life' and 'showed her a new path.'

You're about to write 'Excellent work!' in the margin when you read the final line: 'I will never forget the night he invited me to his hotel room to discuss my thesis.'

The sentence is ambiguous. Yuki is a 32-year-old professional. She wrote this voluntarily and submitted it for your feedback. The professor's name is real. How do you respond?

A learner in your Intermediate class — Carlos — asks for your personal WhatsApp number so he can send you questions about homework. He says: 'The other teacher gave me their number. It's just for homework, I promise.'

Your academy has no formal policy on teacher-learner contact outside of class. Some teachers share their numbers; others don't. Carlos is a respectful, hardworking student who has never crossed a boundary.

You want to be supportive. You also want to maintain professional boundaries. What do you do?

During a pair-work activity, you're monitoring and stop at the table of two learners — Fatima and Aisha, both adult women. They are speaking quietly in their shared L1 instead of English.

This is a monolingual class and your academy's policy is English-only in the classroom. You politely remind them: 'English, please.'

Fatima looks up and says, quietly: 'Teacher, we are talking about the activity. I understand the question in my head but I cannot say it in English yet. Can I please first understand it in my language, and then tell you in English?'

She is not being defiant. She is explaining her cognitive process. The English-only rule is academy policy. What do you say?

Your DoS (Director of Studies) asks you to teach a one-hour demonstration lesson next week for a prospective new student — a 7-year-old beginner who has never studied English. Your DoS says: 'Just show them a fun time. Nothing too academic. We want to sell the school.'

You have zero experience teaching young learners. Your training and experience are entirely with adults and teenagers. Your toolkit of techniques — CCQs, error correction codes, needs analysis — are designed for a completely different developmental stage.

You want to help your DoS. But you also know that a poorly taught demo lesson can do more harm than good — for the child, for the school, and for your own confidence. How do you handle this?

You overhear two teachers in the staff room discussing a learner from your class:

'Oh, you have Ahmed this term? Good luck. He's lazy. His mum does all his homework — everyone knows. Just pass him and get him to the next level. Not our problem.'

Ahmed is a quiet 14-year-old in your Intermediate class. He's never been disruptive. His homework is always perfect — suspiciously so — but his in-class performance is weak. You had noticed the gap but hadn't labelled it as 'laziness' or 'cheating.'

The other teachers' framing of Ahmed is clearly biased and professionally questionable. But they have years more experience than you at this academy. What do you do?

You're in your first year at a new academy. Looking back at the term, you realise that every single dilemma you've faced — from the dominant student in Week 1 to the ethical questions in Week 10 — could have been handled differently with hindsight.

Your mentor teacher — a veteran with 20 years in the classroom — tells you: 'The first year is survival. The second year is reflection. The third year is craft. Give yourself time.'

You have one piece of advice for a new teacher starting next term. It's the distilled wisdom from every scenario you've navigated in this course. What is it?

Choose the principle that best reflects your teaching philosophy.
